claims: Debt when the TDP government took office (June 2014) was about ₹97,000 crore.
Debt by the end of 2018-19 was ₹2,58,928 crore.
Including off-budget borrowings, total debt was about ₹3.62 lakh crore.
claims.context: The ₹2,58,928 crore figure matches AP's own 2018-19 Revised Estimate. For the same date, later Accounts show ₹2,57,510 crore (AP/CAG) and RBI shows ₹2,64,451 crore. No CAG-published off-budget total exists for 2018-19 to check the ₹3.62 lakh crore claim against — CAG's first published AP off-budget figure is ₹26,097 crore, as at 31 March 2020.

claims: Debt on the state's exchequer as on 31.03.2019 was ₹3,75,295 crore.
Debt on the state's exchequer as on 12.06.2024 was ₹9,74,556 crore (reported breakup includes government debt ₹4,38,278 crore and corporation debt ₹2,48,677 crore, plus unpaid dues).
claims.context: These are widened totals (budget debt + corporation borrowings + unpaid bills), so they are not directly comparable to RBI/CAG headline debt. For 31 March 2019, RBI shows ₹2,64,451 crore and CAG ₹2,57,510 crore. For 31 March 2024, RBI shows ₹4,92,568 crore and AP's own accounts ₹4,91,734 crore; CAG's audited off-budget figure was ₹1,28,048 crore at 31 March 2023 — smaller than the white paper's corporation-debt figure. The tabled document is an image-only scan; its full breakup is not machine-readable.

growth_facts: Market loans (SDLs) are the biggest and fastest-growing piece in rupees: ₹1.89 lakh crore (March 2020) → ₹4.24 lakh crore (March 2025 revised estimate) in RBI's series — up 124%.
Loans from the central government grew fastest in proportion: ₹17,763 crore (2020) → ₹48,104 crore (2025 RE), about 2.7 times.
Small-savings (NSSF) securities shrank every single year — ₹11,331 crore (2020) → ₹5,507 crore (2025 RE).

Across CAG's audited span (2016→2023): internal debt grew 2.9×, central loans 2.1×, public-account liabilities 1.4× — and the fastest-growing audited category of all is off-budget borrowing: ₹26,097 crore (2020) → ₹1,28,048 crore (2023), 4.9× in three years.
composition.definitions_note: RBI, CAG and AP's budget books group some components differently (for example what counts as 'loans from the Centre', or bank borrowings), so the same year can show different sub-totals across sources. Categories are shown under each source's own definitions, never merged.

glossary.debt: 'Outstanding debt' is all the money the government has borrowed and not yet repaid — like the total of every loan a family still owes. It is measured on 31 March each year. Solid columns are final audited numbers ('actuals'); lighter columns are the government's own estimates, which usually change later.
glossary.composition: The government does not take one big loan. It borrows in many ways: selling bonds that banks and investors buy, taking loans from the central government and banks — and it also holds money it must return, like its own employees' provident fund savings. This chart shows those pieces.
glossary.offbudget: These are loans the government takes through its corporations, so they do NOT appear in the main debt figure. The government still has to repay them. That is why the national auditor (CAG) counts them separately — and why two people quoting 'the debt' can both be quoting official numbers and still differ.
glossary.guarantees: A guarantee is a promise: if a government corporation cannot repay its loan, the government will pay instead. It is not debt yet — but it becomes debt the day the corporation fails to pay. Think of it as signing as surety for a relative's loan.
glossary.ratio: This compares the debt to the size of AP's whole economy (GSDP — the value of everything the state produces in a year). It is like comparing a family's loans to its yearly income: ₹5 lakh of loans is heavy for a ₹10 lakh income, light for a ₹50 lakh income.
glossary.deficits: A fiscal deficit means the government spent more than it earned that year and borrowed the difference. A revenue deficit is more serious: even the daily running costs — salaries, pensions, interest — were more than income, so the government borrowed just to run the house.
glossary.claims: A white paper is a report a government publishes about its predecessor — a political document, not a neutral audit. We show what each one claimed, next to what the audited records say, so you can compare.
glossary.committed: Before a government can build anything, it must pay what it has already committed — interest on old loans, salaries and pensions. This shows how much of every rupee the state earns is gone on interest alone before a single new decision is taken.
glossary.promised: Each year the Assembly votes a sum for every department. The Accountant General later publishes what was actually spent against each of those votes. The difference is money that was announced but never spent — not corruption, but not delivery either.
glossary.clock: The headline is the most recent figure each official source publishes. They differ because they count different things and are published at different times. Tap any figure to see which document it came from.

residuary_2014_15.label: 2014-15, the ten months of residuary Andhra Pradesh only (2 June 2014 to 31 March 2015)
residuary_2014_15.note: The March 2016 book prints 2014-15 in three columns: two months of undivided Andhra Pradesh, ten months of the residuary state, and the two added together. For any comparison with later years, only the ten-month column is the same state.

per_second.note: This is arithmetic on the interest provision in the state’s own budget for 2025-26, divided evenly across the year. It is not a live measurement, and interest is not actually paid at a constant rate.

caveats: Every figure is the Accounts (audited) reading from AP’s own FRBM book, except 2025-26 which is a Revised Estimate and is marked as such.
The same fiscal year appears in more than one book — first as a Revised Estimate, later as Accounts. Where they differ we show the Accounts figure and name the book it came from.

Two revisions are large enough to matter: 2022-23 revenue receipts fell from ₹1,76,448 crore (RE) to ₹1,57,768 crore (Accounts), and 2022-23 capital expenditure from ₹16,847 crore (RE) to ₹7,244 crore (Accounts).
2018-19 GSDP was revised down from ₹9,33,402 crore to ₹8,62,957 crore between two books, so any ratio for that year moves depending on which book you read.

population.label: Population of Andhra Pradesh

census_2011.note: Census of India 2011 does not publish a single state row for the residuary state of Andhra Pradesh in Table A-1: that release predates the 2014 reorganisation and its state row for code 28 is undivided Andhra Pradesh (84,580,777). The figures above are the exact sum of the 13 official district rows that formed the residuary state in 2014 (Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, East Godavari, West Godavari, Krishna, Guntur, Prakasam, Sri Potti Sriramulu Nellore, Y.S.R., Kurnool, Anantapur, Chittoor). Each district figure is verbatim; only the addition is mine. The result, 49,386,799, is the standard published residuary-AP figure and is corroborated independently: 84,580,777 (undivided AP, Table A-2) minus 35,193,978 (Telangana) = 49,386,799; and the urban total 14,610,410 matches the 14,610 thousand printed for Andhra Pradesh for 2011 in Table 9 of the National Commission on Population report. The 2011 district boundaries above exclude the seven Khammam mandals transferred to Andhra Pradesh later in 2014.

population.caveat: The National Commission on Population projects 49,577 thousand for Andhra Pradesh in 2011, while the Census district rows for the same 13 districts add to 49,386,799. The two NCP figures for AP and Telangana sum exactly to undivided Andhra Pradesh, so about 190 thousand people the Census counted in Telangana are counted in Andhra Pradesh here — consistent with the seven Khammam mandals transferred in 2014. The projected series runs about 0.4% above a Census-anchored one. We use the projection because it is the only official year-by-year series, and we say so on every per-person figure.

promised_vs_spent.coverage_note: Appropriation Accounts are published grant by grant by the Accountant General and audited by the CAG. We now hold 8 years, of which 6 are complete grant by grant and reconcile to the volume's own printed grand total: 2014-15, 2015-16, 2017-18, 2018-19, 2019-20, 2022-23. Four of those fall under the first TDP government and two under the YSRCP government, which is where the published record happens to be readable, not a choice we made. Two further years — 2023-24 and 2024-25 — are held at state totals only, because the grant rows would not extract twice the same way and we would rather show nothing than attach a figure to the wrong department.

missing.why: The file the Accountant General's archive links for this year is not Andhra Pradesh — its title page reads Kerala. We discarded it rather than ingest it, and it is worth reporting to the CAG.
Published, but the summary table would not read the same way twice — grant numbers shifted against grant names on every pass. Needs reading by hand.

Published. Its rows shift diagonally on extraction, each row's expenditure landing as the next row's total. It is also the one volume printed in crore rather than thousands, so anyone reading it must not apply the usual conversion.
State totals held and reconciled. Grant rows did not extract reliably.

promised_vs_spent.how_to_help: cag.gov.in → Principal Accountant General (A&E), Andhra Pradesh → Annual Accounts → Appropriation Accounts. Set the year filter and turn on the Archive switch. The page we need in each volume is the "Summary of Appropriation Accounts" in the front matter.
promised_vs_spent.validation: 160 reconciliation checks across the four newly added years: every grant row sums to the printed total, in every section, to the last printed digit. Nothing was adjusted to make anything match. Two real transcription errors were caught this way and corrected at source — a Public Debt line attached to the wrong grant, and saving and excess columns swapped on whole blocks.
promised_vs_spent._arithmetic_note: Every percentage here is exactly what you get by dividing the two rupee figures printed beside it. We round the rupee figures first and then divide, rather than dividing the unrounded originals, so that a reader recomputing from what is on screen gets our answer.
promised_vs_spent._units_note: These volumes print '(₹ in thousand)' and group digits two at a time, so 2,31,92,58,09 is ₹23,192.58 crore. The 2021-22 volume alone prints in crore. Every figure here carries the raw printed string beside it.

tenure_boundary_note: Fiscal years do not line up with governments. The TDP government took office on 8 June 2014, so 2014-15 is ten months of it (and the two months before that are undivided Andhra Pradesh). The YSRCP government took office on 30 May 2019, so 2019-20 is ten months of it. The TDP-led NDA government took office on 12 June 2024, so 2024-25 is ten months of it. We label each year by the government that held office for most of it, and say so here rather than hiding it.
